metadata.title: Concept Drift: Why Good Models Get Worse Over Time — Short
metadata.continuity: Portrait-native derivative of the approved Concept Drift explainer; not a crop.
metadata.methodological_boundary: Data drift and concept drift are distinct; warning signs require investigation; not every performance drop is drift and not every distribution change requires retraining.
metadata.production_gate: Shortened narration and vertical beat plan approved; review rendering authorized; clean final master not authorized.

beats.narration_text: Hi, my name is Ushasvi Rachel, and this video is about concept drift and why machine-learning models can become less accurate over time. A model can perform well when it is trained and still become less reliable later. That does not necessarily mean it was poorly built. The world around it may have changed.

shot.visual_intent: Integrated presenter introduction and vertical lifecycle timeline.

beats.narration_text: Concept drift occurs when the statistical relationship between a model's inputs and its target changes over time. The model may still run normally, using the same code and parameters. But the relationship it learned during training may no longer describe current behavior as well.

Consider a hypothetical model that predicts which customers are likely to buy a product. During training, high website engagement may be strongly associated with purchases. After deployment, customer behavior changes. People may continue browsing frequently but purchase less because prices, economic conditions, or shopping habits have changed. Engagement still exists, but its relationship with purchasing is now different.

shot.visual_intent: Stacked training and later-period customer relationship graphics.

beats.narration_text: This is different from data drift. Data drift means the distribution of input features changes. For example, customers may begin visiting the website more frequently. Concept drift means the relationship between those inputs and the target changes. Frequent visits may no longer predict purchases as strongly. The two can occur together, but they are not the same thing.

shot.visual_intent: Full-width stacked data-drift and concept-drift comparison.

beats.narration_text: A deployed model can continue producing predictions while its real-world performance quietly declines. Warning signs include declining production performance, changing feature distributions, and changing error patterns across time periods or user groups. These are reasons to investigate, not automatic proof of concept drift.

shot.visual_intent: Vertical healthy-service versus degrading-performance track and warning cards.

beats.narration_text: Teams should monitor inputs, predictions, outcomes, and errors over time. When a change appears, diagnosis comes first. Retraining may be appropriate, but every feature-distribution change does not automatically require it. Any updated model should also be validated before deployment.

shot.visual_intent: Stacked monitor, diagnose, retrain-if-appropriate, validate workflow.

beats.narration_text: Concept drift is also different from overfitting. Overfitting means a model learned its training data too specifically. Concept drift means the environment, or the relationship being modeled, changed after training. Both can reduce real-world performance, but they are different problems.

Deployment is not the end of the machine-learning lifecycle. Good systems continue monitoring whether the conditions behind their predictions still hold. A good model today is not guaranteed to be a good model tomorrow.

shot.visual_intent: Vertical lifecycle loop and exact closing takeaway.
